title: Playing for Huey and Earl Long
summary: DeDroit says he played at Huey Long's campaigns and for Earl Long at the Baton Rouge mansion, and that both liked musicians.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Yes. But only when I was playing at the Club Forest. I was playing with Marty Rapp. And he was campaigning. And we couldn't leave the bandstand, well we couldn't get too far away, because every, after that, whenever he finished something, he said, I'll take you back to the Club Forest and Marty Rapp's off, and we danced from a bandstand and played something, you know. He got free music all the time between his speeches. But I never did meet Huey Long. Earl Long, I played a favorite. I used to go up there and play at his mansion up in Baton Rouge, you know.
Was he a music fancier himself, Earl Long?
Earl Long liked musicians. He catered to them.
Huey had that reputation also. I'm talking about yours.

Earl Long. Mrs. Long was a very fine woman and she liked me because of my conduct and so and so. Although they say that Earl didn't drink, he looked to me like he was loaded on something. But it didn't bother me any. But Earl Long, I mean Huey Long, loved musicians. One time LSU did as an oboe player.

You could have got free tuition and clothes and money, but come up there playing the band, he couldn't find an oboe player. He loved musicians. If he liked you, you were him, because he was a dictator. I never respected him. He ran that road in the hotel. But I never had the pleasure of playing, but I played for Earl Long, I played for Mrs. Earl quite regularly, unless you'd give a dance up at the mansion, to this farm, sent us home loaded with cakes and food. You paid for it, you paid for it.
